en: Here, it was previously stated that one should perform the fire offering (*homa*) for the sake of pacification and so forth. Thus, as it was said before: "Therefore, consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) has not been taught here without the mandala and the fire offering."
Therefore, out of a desire for the welfare of the disciple, one should properly perform the rite of fire-oblation (homa).

There is no teaching for this consecration that is devoid of the maṇḍala and the fire offering (homa). Therefore, one who desires to benefit the disciples should correctly perform the ritual of the fire offering.
Due to the diversity of sentient beings, [the types of] families are infinite;
according to the distinction of karma, there are four kinds. This is the defining characteristic of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).

Sentient beings are infinite when divided by species; they are of five types when divided by lineage; they are of four types when divided by karma. Such is the defining characteristic of what is called the "fire-pit."

Having set aside what has been said at length, I shall now state in brief the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to its divisions, such as those for rites of pacification (śāntika) and so forth.

Having completely set aside the many various explanations, I shall here summarize them well; I will describe the characteristics of the hearth according to the distinctions of tranquility and so forth.
For rites of pacification (śāntika), the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is circular, with an altar featuring a lotus with filaments;
upon it is placed an eight-fingered wheel situated in the center of an eight-petalled lotus.
The hearth for pacification is circular; its rim is adorned with lotuses and gold. In the center, one should arrange an eight-petaled lotus and an eight-finger-width wheel.
Having left a space of four finger-breadths all around on the horizontal plane,
one should fashion an altar-platform measuring four finger-breadths both in width and in height.
It is one cubit all around, excluding four finger-widths; the rim is four finger-widths, and its width is equal to its height.
For rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika), it should be square or octagonal, measuring two cubits;
with an eight-petalled lotus in the center and jewels measuring six finger-breadths.
Having left a space of eight finger-breadths on all sides, both in width and in height,
the altar (vedi) is to be encircled on every side with a border of eight finger-breadths.
The *kuṇḍa* for pacifying (*śāntika*) and enriching (*pauṣṭika*) rites should likewise be slightly tilted downward.

For the rite of increasing (*vāśika*), it may be square or octagonal, measuring two cubits on each side. Leaving a space of eight finger-widths all around, there should be an eight-petaled lotus in the center with a jewel six finger-widths in size. It is completely encircled by a rim (*kha-khyer*) eight finger-widths wide, equal in measure to the [central] power.
In the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*), the dimensions of the pit, the altar, and so forth are like those of the pacificatory (*śāntika*) fire-pit;
likewise, in the rite of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), it is desired to be the same, while in subjugation, it is considered to be shaped like a female organ (*bhaga*).

For empowerment, the hearths for pacifying, enriching, and subjugating are likewise [prepared], though the latter is slightly wider than the enriching one. The hearth for pacifying on the altar and so forth should be explained as being like the [standard] hearth; it is likewise asserted for summoning.
In the rite of summoning, it has a central lotus with a goad placed in its center;
in the rite of malevolent magic, it is said to resemble a single-pointed vajra.

In the center of the lotus, for the sake of power (*vaśya*), one should visualize it as resembling a vulva (*bhaga*); in the center of the summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), one should place a hook (*aṅkuśa*) having the form of a single-pointed vajra.
On a portion of ground that is parched and saline, there should be a foul-smelling flower and so forth;
the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is triangular, slanted, and measures twenty finger-breadths.
Regarding the rites of forceful activity (*abhicāra*), it should be described: on a ground that is harsh and stony, there is a triangular hearth-pit with a width of twenty finger-breadths.
In the center of the pit, there is a sharp eight-finger-long vajra fixed upon a trident;
it is smeared with funeral ashes, donkey dung, and other sacrificial offerings, with its head pointing north.
Having abandoned three finger-breadths from the circumference measured by its height,
there is an outer altar (vedi) of three finger-breadths, which is turned away from the interior.

Excluding three finger-breadths [from the top], its width and height are equal in measure. The outer rim, which turns outward, is three finger-breadths wide. In the center of the base, there is a sharp vajra eight finger-breadths long, with its tip pointing north. One should scatter burnt ashes, goat droppings, foul-smelling flowers, and so forth.
That pit for all rites is equal in size to the pit for pacification;
however, it should resemble a full-blown lotus and be encircled by a garland of vajras.
The hearth for all activities is equal to the hearth of pacification; yet it is like a fully blossomed lotus, its rim encircled by a garland of vajras.
The center is presided over by the self surrounded by the vajras known as Vajra, Ratna, Abja, and Viśva, and adorned with an eight-spoked wheel.
In the center, situated in equipoise, are the vajra, jewel, and lotus, completely surrounded by a crossed-vajra, and a beautiful eight-spoked wheel.
For pacification (śānti) and subjugation (vaśya), the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is in the eastern direction; for nourishment (puṣṭi), in the southern direction;
for attraction (ākarṣaṇa), in the western direction; and for the remaining rite, malevolent magic (abhicāraka), in the [northern] direction.

The hearths for pacification and magnetizing are in the east; the hearth for enrichment is in the northern direction; that for summoning is explained as being in the south; and the one for wrathful activities is in the direction of Yama.
For pacification, nourishment, subjugation, and malevolent rites, the sites for the sacrificial pit,
as well as the plaster, clay, flowers, and perfumes, are white, yellow, reddish, and black respectively.

On the sites for the hearths of pacification, enrichment, likewise magnetizing, and wrathful activity, there should be ointments, clay, flowers, and incense that are white, yellow, red, and black, respectively.
The measurement for the lower portion is considered to be half the measurement of the horizontal part.
The altar (vedī) should have the same shape as its respective fire-pit (kuṇḍa); in the case of attraction and subjugation, it should be like the ground and so forth.

Whatever the measurement of the Chinese portion may be, half of that is held to be the depth. Each has its own hearth-shape and rim; it is like the mastery over the earth and so forth without exception.

The enclosures and the sacrificial pits consist of dust, according to the distinction of the ritual acts; the preceptor likewise should possess the appropriate attire and the timing for each occasion.

According to the classification of activities, one should arrange the nature of the colored powders upon the hearths; likewise, the preceptor shall be present at the appropriate time, stationed within each respective curtain.
Thus concludes the procedure for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the fire-pit.
A vessel made of copper or bronze is recommended, as is one made of nimba wood;
furthermore, its handle should be fashioned from the wood of sacrificial trees.
Those made of iron, gold, or copper, as well as those of the nature of clay, or even those made from sacrificial wood—these are suitable; furthermore, their handles...
It is considered to be twenty-four finger-breadths in measure and circular;
its thickness, from the top of the handle upward, should be such that it can be grasped by the fist of a Vajra [or similar hand].
It is held to be circular, measuring twenty-four finger-widths; it is suitable to be grasped with the vajra-fist and so forth, and is indeed for meditation.
On a square cloth measuring four finger-breadths,
there is a square depression two finger-breadths wide, with its center marked by a vajra.
At the tip of the stalk, the petals are four finger-breadths wide and square; they are also two finger-breadths deep and square, and are marked in their center by a vajra.

The vajra, six finger-breadths in length, is considered to be marked with jewels at the base of the staff.
The handle of the *śruva* ladle is like that of the *pātrī*; below the handle, there is a *vajra*.

At the base of the handle, a *vajra* marked with jewels is desired, measuring six finger-breadths. The *sruk* ladle has a handle like that of the *sruva*, and at its base, it is likewise marked with a *vajra*.
The *śruva* ladle is one cubit in height all around and made of solid material;
its tip has the form of a two-finger-width lotus petal with a vajra set in its center.
In the absence of a *pātrī* and a *śruva*, [the offering] is praised when performed using five fingers; it is better than using three, or otherwise.
If the large and small ladles are not available, others have taught that one may complete the auspicious rite by employing the five fingers and the three [fingers] joined together.
Thus concludes the rule for the *pātrī* and the *sruva*.
Thus concludes the ritual for the filling and pouring ladles.
Fuel-sticks produced from milky trees such as the *aśvattha* and *plakṣa*,
along with their leaves, cut evenly, of the finest quality, and measuring one span (*vitasti*) in length, are to be offered.

*Āśvattha*, *dadima*, *plakṣa*, and so forth—trees that produce milk, along with their leaves and sap; their tops cut level to a height of one span, moist, unblemished, and pure at the tips; smeared with milk, honey, and clarified butter, [held] over both fires;
focused, sprinkled with white perfumes, and joined in pairs.

Melted butter, wild honey, and sesame oil are poured; it is perfumed with the scent of white *kunda* flowers. With fuel sticks of *yava* grass, which have become pure through union and equilibrium, one should perform the fire offering (*homa*).
Those that are broken, crooked, thin, thick, lacking a tip, double-tipped,
shattered, split, or infested with worms are to be rejected.
A curved [lip] causes misfortune; a short one immediately turns away knowledge;
a protruding one causes disease; and a thick one [destroys] all prosperity.

One that is withered, burnt, unfit for sacrifice, or otherwise unfit is said to be "other" [than the proper fuel]. One should know that what is to be burned is explained as being other than those that are shriveled, coarse, thick, broken at the tip, two-tipped, dry, crooked, or undesirable.
Dadhi, milk, excellent food, dūrvā grass, lāyā, barley,
sesame seeds, darbha grass, banyan leaves, white flowers, saffron, and sandalwood— [these are required].
Curd and milk as the supreme food, parched rice, barley, and sesame; *kuśa* grass, *cūta* leaves, and the filaments of white flowers.
The resin of the priyaṅgu flower and these sacrificial substances should be offered as they are available, anointed with honey and clarified butter, during rites for pacification.

Sandalwood, *priyaṅgu*, and flowers are said to be the fire-offerings for the riverbank; one should perform the burnt offering with whatever is available. For pacification, honey and ghee are used as the offerings.
Those very same fuel-sticks, when smeared with milk, curd, and clarified butter, are the *kāraga* cups.
Those produced from the hands of the drum-player are the size of a handful, smeared with yellow fragrances;
they are made from those very same trees for the rite of enrichment, measuring one cubit in length, mixed with milk, curd, and ghee, and held in the hand while being anointed with yellow fragrance.
Excellent food, rice-balls, curd-rice, karṇikāra flowers, and great sesame seeds.
The lotus, the śrīphala fruit, śāli rice, and vrīhi rice;
likewise, the finest food, balls of curd-rice, karṇikāra, and great sesame; the lotus, the śrīphala, śāli grains, and various seeds.
With *nāgakesara* and *śatapuṣpa*, [these are used] for rites of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*).
All sacrificial materials mixed with the three sweets, according to availability.
Likewise, for the rite of enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), it is desired that the sacrificial substances be mixed with equal parts of *nāgakeśara*, *śatapatra* flowers, and the three sweets.
The campaka, aśoka, bakula, priyaṅgu, lakuca, and so forth.

Fresh *nāgakesara* flowers with five petals, as well as *campaka*, *aśoka*, *bakula*, *priyaṅgu*, *laguḍa*, mango, and so forth— red fruits and flowers of these five-fingered yellow *nāgakesara* trees are the sacrificial substances for the rite of subjugation (*vaśyaka*).
It is the same for attraction; however, the thorn should be in the shape of a goad.

Gold, red fruits, flowers, and substances for the fire-oblation are for the rite of power (*vaśīkaraṇa*); the same applies to the rite of summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), except that [the latter] uses thorny [wood] in the shape of a hook.
Palāśa, udumbara, plakṣa, aśvattha, khadira, and śamī.
Fresh fuel-sticks of Apāmārga, Arka, Kāśmarya, Āmra, Vaikaṅkata, and Vaṭa—
each measuring a span (pradeśa)— are to be taken from these trees.
In all ritual acts, the sacrificial twigs should be single-pointed and provided with leaves.

For all rites, one should take these fresh sacrificial woods: *udumbara*, *bālaśa*, *pākṣāśvattha*, *sinduka*, *samī*, *āmrātaka*, *arka*, *kashmāmra*, *bījakam*, *kadamba*, and *nyagrodha*. An oblation of a single finger-breadth in length shall be offered.
Mustard seeds, pungent oil, blood, neem leaves, and black mustard.
The dung of camels and other animals, salt, excrement, urine, funeral pyres,
living beings, hair, thorns, the wings and bones of crows and other birds, and dust from the feet [are all inauspicious].
In that battle, the sacrificial materials consisted of human flesh, fat, and the like;
by means of these substances, the limbs of the enemy were severed into pieces.
In rites of sorcery (*abhicāruka*), each [of these substances] should be smeared with poison, blood, and salt:

white mustard seeds, hot sesame oil, blood, *nimba* leaves, *kacchaka*, the dung of camels and the like, ashes from a funeral pyre, lime, hair, thorns, the feathers of crows and the like, bone-dust, the dust of feet, and substances such as human flesh and fat—these materials [should be applied] to the body of the enemy.
Once it has been cut into pieces, each fragment becomes a sacrificial offering that intensely incinerates with poison and blood.
Whatever substance is used for pacification and nourishment, as well as whatever food one consumes oneself;

One should constantly offer guggulu resin and the exudation of *śāli* trees, all of which has been smeared with clarified butter and accompanied by abundant *svāhā*, according to the specific distinctions of the mantras.
The offering of perfumes, flowers, and so forth should be performed through the application of ritual action.

Whatever substances are used for pacifying or enriching, even those one consumes oneself—clarified butter, asafoetida, guggulu, and saffron—all these should be combined constantly. With the mantra of Śvāsapati, one should perform many burnt offerings (*homa*) for the purpose of causing division. Fragrances, flowers, and ritual offerings should be prepared according to the application of the specific activity.
Thus concludes the rule for the sacrificial substances.
This is the ritual procedure for the substances of the fire offering.
For rites of pacification, the fuel— produced from trees that are components of the sacrifice— should be less than the sacrificial pit, mixed with wild cow-dung, and free from living organisms.
From the hearth of the firewood of peace, I desire a sacrificial wood that is somewhat shorter; together with it, I seek the heavy oxen of the wilderness, which are free from living beings.

As it has been said: "In rites for nourishment (pauṣṭika), one should avoid the fuel prescribed [for other rites] and instead use forest cow-dung; and from one's own sacrificial pit, the quantity should be less than the standard measure, along with the fruit [of the rite]."
Except for the cow dung from the wilderness of the forest of the Extensive [Abhidharma], the teaching was presented exactly as it was spoken; together with its own fuel, it is equal to the fruit.
For subjugation, one should use fuel from the *nimba* or *amlavṛkṣa* trees along with their flowers;
for plowing, it should be known that thorny wood is required; and for malevolent rites (*abhicāruka*), it should be dried.
For magnetizing, [use] wood that is sour and possesses flowers; for summoning, it is said to be thorny wood; and for the rite of forceful action, it is dry wood.
That which is produced from trees that are pungent, thorny, or foul-smelling, as well as that produced from a funeral pyre,
or the dung of donkeys, camels, and the like— all that is for use in all rites.

Avoid those that are thorny, bitter, or foul-smelling, as well as trees grown in charnel grounds; likewise, avoid the *bodbu* and *rnga mo* trees. For all ritual activities, one must avoid all such [trees].
Thus is the procedure regarding fuel.
Thus concludes the ritual for the firewood.
Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, being peaceful and dressed in white garments and so forth,
one should sit facing east on a bull-hide in the lotus posture at the time of dusk.
Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, clad in white garments and the like, facing east at dusk, one should sit upon an excellent seat, a lotus throne.

Having meditated upon the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) in accordance with the rite, endowed with loving-kindness and compassion, and observing silence through the yoga corresponding to the rite, one should perform the pacification (*śānti*).

Establish it permanently in accordance with the ritual action; endowed with loving-kindness and compassion, practice correctly with a peaceful mind through the yoga that accords with the ritual action.
Seated upon an auspicious throne, facing north on the full moon day,
wearing yellow garments and the like, and being well-nourished, he should commence the rite for prosperity in the forenoon.
Beginning from the full moon, one clad in yellow robes and the like, facing east in the forenoon, should remain seated in the auspicious posture.
Seated upon a high, comfortable, and beautiful throne in the vajraparyaṅka posture,
facing west and dressed in red garments and so forth, one should effect subjugation as described.
Wearing red garments and so forth for the empowerment, facing west upon a high seat and remaining in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, it is taught that one should act with both bliss and joy.
All [methods] are equal in their power of attraction; however, the attainment of higher bliss is desired [through this one].
Furthermore, one should perform the propitiation of the deity facing westward.
In all cases of summoning, they are identical; nevertheless, one desires to face upward. For the purpose of pleasing the deities as well, one should correctly apply the gaze toward the west.
Clad in blue garments and the like, wrathful, or with clothes drenched in blood, seated facing the south upon a firm seat; or else—
Wearing blue garments for the wrathful rites or any other cloth stained with blood, facing the direction of Yama, one should sit upon a firm seat or rough ground.
He has firmly mounted the chest of his adversary;
having pressed foot against foot, he sits down, deprived of his seat.
One should remain with the image of the object of accomplishment firmly and completely established upon one's chest, or else sit without a seat, pressing foot against foot.
At midday or at midnight, on a single lunar day of the two dark fortnights, one who performs malevolent magic should practice it with his teeth clenched and his eyebrows knit together. ||o||
On the first day of the dark fortnight, at midday or at midnight, one should practice the rite of Kṛṣṇa while gnashing the teeth, knitting the eyebrows, and contracting the brow.
Facing the northeast and seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, he [should perform the rite] for the pillar and the delusion [deity] with the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* in a square sacrificial pit.
One should gaze with eyes fixed and mind composed; likewise, assuming the vajra posture, one should fashion a square hearth by appending the mantra *boṣaṭ* at its end.
Adorned with yellow and white ornaments, established in the ritual posture of nourishment (puṣṭi),
and facing the southeast, one should likewise apply the dung of camels and other such animals for the rite of eradication (uccāṭana).
Adorned with black and white ornaments, whatever assembly of deities resides in the full [mandala], one should likewise direct them toward the fire;

the offering here consists of a mixture of poison, the feathers of crows and other such birds, combined with the *vidarbhaṇa* [mantra-interlacing]. One should smear the [substances] with mantras upon a black and white [surface].
Adorned with white and black, it is drawn with poison; the substances and mantras are these: the supreme wings of the *khva-ta* and so forth, perfectly endowed with the alternating phrases.
In this case, [the drawing] is joined with the writing of mantras such as "Expel so-and-so! HŪṂ PHAṬ! starting from the wings of a crow and so forth.
Likewise, for the rite of hatred, one faces the southwest and uses pungent oil, poison, and the like.
Here, it is joined with the writing of mantras such as "Expel so-and-so! HŪṂ PHAṬ! Similarly, for the rite of causing division, one faces the southwest (Nairṛtya).
The letter *la* is the foot, inverted, adorned with yellow and black.
That which faces every direction and intermediate direction is straight; that which stands in another direction or intermediate direction is otherwise.

One should sit there with the feet turned back, adorned with yellow and black [pigments]. One should draw [the design] with hot sesame oil and poison. In every direction and intermediate direction, one should remain facing whichever direction or intermediate direction one is oriented toward.

Or, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because the directions have no fixed status, one should perform everything exactly as the mind, established in its natural state, is concentrated with matured ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*); such is the rule regarding the characteristics of the practitioner (*sādhaka*).

Furthermore, since in ultimate reality there is no autonomous position of one's own, one should perform all actions exactly as they are, endowed with meditative concentration and a mind characterized by the great pride of that very certainty.
A vessel made of gold, silver, stone, copper, wood, clay, or mother-of-pearl,
or a conch shell, or a leaf-cup, may be used for the arghya, sprinkling, and other such rites.
Gold, silver, stone, copper, wood, clay, fish-skins, conch shells, leaf-fans, foot-washing basins, vessels for sprinkling perfumes, and bowls for water offerings.
The knower of mantras should recite water mixed with barley, milk, white perfumes, and other ingredients, ending with "svāhā," using his own personal mantra for the purpose of pacification.
Having prepared milk and white fragrances and so forth at that peaceful site, the mantra-knower, the master of mantras, should recite over the water a mantra ending with *svāhā*.

For rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika), one should recite over water— mixed with sesame seeds and curd, and consecrated with perfumes and other substances— the mantra of the deity ending with the syllable Om (praṇava).

There, one should extensively mix sesame and yogurt, and having prepared yellow perfumes and so forth, one should perform the recitation of one's own mantra with the syllable *oṃ* at its end over water.
With the mantra ending in *hoḥ*, one should consecrate water with red sandalwood paste for subjugation (*vaśya*);
for attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*), one should recite [the mantra] ending in *jaḥ* seven times over the water.

For the empowerment, one should perform the recitation of the mantra ending with the syllable *hoḥ* for the red scent and so forth; for the summoning, [one should perform it] seven times with the mantra ending in the syllable *jjaḥ*.

In rites of sorcery (abhicāruka), one should recite over water a mantra ending with the syllable *phaṭ*, combined with blood, cow’s urine, and kodrava grain, along with black and foul-smelling substances.

For the rite of forceful activity (*abhicāra*), one should recite the mantra ending in *phaṭ* over water that contains blood, cow urine, and goat’s urine, and is endowed with black and foul-smelling substances.
In every case, water mixed with fragrance, flowers, darbha grass, lāja,
and sesame seeds should be poured according to the specific rite and as is appropriate.
One should prepare as much water as is available, endowed with incense, flowers, *kuśa* grass, parched grain, and sesame seeds, in accordance with the ritual action.
This is the procedure for the *argha* offering. Oṃ.
Likewise, one should consecrate the vessel for the *argha* offering and the water vessel for all-purpose rites with the *sārvakarmika* mantra and their respective mantras.
The offering water vessel, and likewise the vessel for all-purpose water, and the mantra for the all-purpose water, should be consecrated with one's own mantra.
Having placed those two vessels on the left side,
he sprinkles the sacrificial fuel and wood with water held in his right hand.
With two lotus vessels arranged on the left side, water is poured into them; holding them with the right hand, one should sprinkle the sacrificial wood and other items for purification.
One should personally place other sacrificial substances as well on the right side;
however, for killing, driving away, and summoning, the sprinkling and the ritual placement (nyāsa) are performed in reverse.
The substances to be burned should be placed to one's own right; however, for the rites of killing, expelling, and summoning, the placement of the *argha* offering should be reversed.
The ritual for settling [the site].

For pacification, the fire should be from a grove of milk-trees (kṣīravṛkṣa) or one that has been beneficial; for nourishment, it should be from a forest fire, a kitchen fire, or one produced in the palace of a king or a nobleman.

Whether it be a fire from a cow-dung fuel stick used for pacification, or any fire in the wilderness; or a fire that has spread through a great forest, or a fire arising in the palace of a king and so forth—
For subjugation, [the fire] comes from the house of a Vaiśya or a courtesan; for plowing, from an actor or a traveler;
for cruel rites, it is born from the house of a Caṇḍāla, or produced from bone or stone.

This very same [procedure] applies even for the forceful summoning (*krūrākarṣa*) and for all other rites according to their respective requirements: for subjugation, from a house of outcasts, prostitutes, or the *rje'u* caste; for summoning, from the work of dancers, guests, and so forth; for fierce rites, from a cremation ground, bone, or stone; and for summoning with force, from a fire originating in the house of a *caṇḍāla*. This itself applies accordingly to all such fierce rites.
Thus ends the chapter on the characteristics of fire.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the characteristic of fire.
Then, having taken up the fire and established it in a pure vessel,

Having offered the bali and protected [the site] preceded by the ringing of the bell, one should then take up the fires and place them correctly in pure vessels; the bali should be given and protection performed, with the bell itself being rung beforehand.
Then again, with the three-syllabled mantra of Vighnāntaka.

Having offered the water for honor (argha), and so forth, with water consecrated by that [mantra], one should again offer the water for honor, the water for the feet, and so on, using the mantra of Vighnāntaka and the three syllables; and likewise with those [mantras] and the water consecrated by recitation.
Having sprinkled water three times with [water] held on the tip of a blade of kuśa grass, [he should sprinkle] the south.
In rites of sorcery (abhicāruka), however, one should perform all [acts] such as the water-offering (argha) with the left hand;

holding [the vessel] with the tips of *kuśa* grass, one should sprinkle [it] three times while circling to the right. In rites of sorcery, however, all [acts] such as the water-offering and so forth should be performed with the left hand.
Then, having thrown it into the sacrificial pit along with dry grass, one should milk it.
Reciting "Oṃ jvala 2 hūṃ," the mantra-practitioner, using air fanned by a whisk, should thoroughly insert fire along with *skam-po* grass into the hearth;
while reciting "Oṃ jvala jvala hūṃ," [he should do so] with the wind arising from the whisk.
And with ghee placed in a sacrificial ladle, over which the *kulahṛd* mantra has been recited seven times.

With that, one should kindle the fire with pungent oil for the purpose of killing; having recited the seven essence-mantras of the family, one should ignite the oblation-ladle resting there with clarified butter. With that, in a fire perfectly ablaze, [one uses] pungent sesame oil for the rite of slaying.
A fresh, unbroken blade of *kuśa* grass, green and the size of a cow's ear.
And [the grass] is consecrated with the mantra: *oṃ vajrasattva āḥ*.
Fresh *kuśa* grass, unbroken, green, and about the size of a cow's ear, is completely recited over with the mantra: *oṃ vajrasattva āḥ*.
First, the practitioner should place two fresh blades of kuśa grass on the left side.

Having placed two *kuśa* grasses on the altar with their tips pointing eastward for the practitioner, and their bases pointing westward toward Yama—the direction of the Lord of Death—[the practitioner] should first hold them individually in his left hand, facing west. Then, [he should place one] with its tip pointing east and [the other] with its base pointing west.

Then, one should cover the kuśa grass with its tips pointing north using kuśa grass with its tips pointing east; this is according to the sequence for the fire-pits (kuṇḍa) used for rites of enrichment, subjugation, and malevolent sorcery. [The Tibetan: Then, the tips [of the kuśa] point north; thereafter, one should cover the fire-pit with kuśa grass. For the rites of enrichment, subjugation, and malevolent sorcery, one should cover the fire-pits in their proper order. [The Sanskrit: uttarāgraṃ tataḥ kuśaṃ pūrvāgraiś chādayet kuśaiḥ | puṣṭivaśyābhicāreṣu kuṇḍeṣu tu yathākramam || 10 ||
Likewise, with its tip pointing north, its tip pointing west, and its tip pointing south.
Likewise, one should first place two blades of kuśa grass on the left side of the altar.
The tips [of the kuśa grass] point north and west; likewise, the tips point south. First, from the left, two kuśa blades are placed for the rim in that same manner.

And here, the conventional designation of directions such as "east" and so forth is made in relation to the practitioner's own orientation; for in the ultimate sense, directions do not exist as real entities. Then:
"Having produced the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) by means of the seed-syllable of one's own tutelary deity, the knower of mantras..."
But having recognized the blazing fire, one should cultivate the meditation on selflessness in its midst.
From the seed-syllable of one's own tutelary deity of mantra, one should generate the hearth; having recognized the blazing fires, one should meditate on selflessness in their midst.
Then, having produced from the syllable *raṃ* a triangular fire,
[one should visualize] the deity situated upon a lotus and sun in its center, arisen from the seed-syllable *ruṃ*.
Then, in the center of the fire generated from the syllable RAṂ in the form of a triangle, [is] that which has arisen from the seed-syllable RAṂ situated upon a lotus and a sun disk.
Dwarfish with a protruding belly, stout, three-faced, and radiant with six arms;
wearing a crown of matted hair, three-eyed, bearded, and clad in a sacred thread.

Short-limbed, with a protruding belly and well-developed muscles; three-faced and six-armed, blazing in splendor; possessing three eyes and a crown of matted locks; and holding a lute for the sake of offering.
Adorned with complexion, garments, ornaments, and jewels according to his karma,
his two graceful arms embrace his own natural consort.
He holds a staff and a water-pot in his left hands, and likewise an akṣamālā and the gesture of fearlessness in his right hands.

His body color, robes, and ornaments are adorned in accordance with his activity. With his first two hands, he playfully and perfectly embraces his own radiance. In his left [hands], he holds a staff and a water-pot; in his right, a rosary and the gesture of granting fearlessness.

Having thus visualized the fire, which is endowed with the Lord of the Family of the Seal of the Garland of Consciousness Rays (*vijñānaraśmimālāmudrā*) and whose heart is empowered by the fire-maṇḍala of the seed-syllable *ruṃ*, one should [visualize] the Knowledge Being (*jñānasattva*) Fire—identical to the Commitment Being (*samayasattva*)—arriving from the southeastern direction in the sky, surrounded by a host of seers. His principal face has the same body color as the [Commitment Being]; if that is white, his right and left faces are black and red; if yellow, red, or green, they are blue and white.
Having seen [the deity] blue, white, or red, one should perform the invocation by moving the right thumb and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) with this mantra:
Oṃ, come, come, O Great Being, God, Sage, Best of the Twice-born!
Having accepted this oblation as food, be present here!

Having thus invoked [the deity] and dispelled the obstacles that have arrived along with him by means of Yamārya and the others, one should perform the rites of attraction, entry, binding, and gratification in their proper order, while those same [deities] utter *jaḥ*, *hūṃ*, *vaṃ*, and *hoḥ*. Likewise, one should meditate on the seed-syllable *raṃ* itself, which resides within a fire-maṇḍala and is endowed with the light-rays of consciousness and the seal of expansion, at the heart.

By means of the hook of light rays from the seed syllable at the heart of the *samayasattva*, the wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*) Agni—identical to the *samayasattva*—emerges from the southeast corner, surrounded by a host of ṛṣis; his primary face corresponds in color to his body, and if that [body] is white, his right and left faces are black and red respectively.

Having visualized yellow, red, and green as blue and white, and blue as white and red, one should invite [the deity] by moving the right thumb with the *abhaya* gesture and reciting this mantra: Oṃ āye hi mahābhūtadevī śrīdvijasa-tama grīhitāhuti.

With the words, "O Mahāra, please come here," he is invited; together with him, the obstructors such as Yamāntaka who have arrived are expelled. Then, by reciting "jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ," one performs the summoning, entry, binding, and pleasing in their proper sequence.

Then, one should offer the *argha* with the mantra: *oṃ āḥ ruṃ arghaṃ pratīccha hūṃ*. By substituting the word *argha* with "water for the feet" (*pādya*) and so forth, one should offer the water for the feet, the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the sprinkling water (*abhyukṣaṇa*). Then, according to the specific ritual action, one should worship with flowers and other offerings, as well as with secret worships (*guhyapūjā*).

Then, one should present the water for offerings with the mantra *oṃ āḥ hūṃ arghaṃ pratīccha hūṃ*. By substituting *pādyaṃ* and so forth in place of the word *arghaṃ*, one should also offer the water for the feet, the water for the face, and the sprinkling of purification. Furthermore, one should worship with flowers and other items corresponding to the specific ritual activity, as well as with secret offerings.
In this regard,
the sequence for the *argha* offering and so forth is as follows:
with three bundles of *kuśa* grass, one should sprinkle water three times into the first vessel.
One should perform the ritual rinsing (ācamana) right there with water over which the *sarvakṛt* mantra has been recited.

With a small bundle of *kuśa* grass, one should perform three *prokṣaṇa* (sprinklings) into the first vessel; having recited [the mantra] over all of them with water, one should offer the *pādya* (water for the feet) right there.

Having taken up a flower with the index finger and formed a downward-facing fist, one should release the fingers in sequence: the little finger, the ring finger, the middle finger, and the index finger.
Having grasped a flower with the index finger of a fist turned downward, one releases the ring finger, the middle finger, and the index finger in succession. This is the *daṃṣṭrā* (tooth) mudrā.
One should offer the *argha* with the first conch, while the second is for the recipient;
then, with the opening of the vajra-añjali gesture, one should give the *pādya* with the third.
Second is the conch-offering water; it is to be offered individually as a second [offering], by opening the vajra-vase. Third, the face-cleansing water is to be offered.
Having grasped a flower with the fist by means of the thumb and index finger,
one should rotate the fingers three times in succession in the presence of the Buddhas.
And one should release the index finger, the middle finger, the ring finger, and the little finger; thus it is traditionally taught.

The flowers held by the dry hand—the fist formed by the index, middle, ring, and little fingers—are rotated three times in succession before the Buddhas. Then, the index, middle, ring, and little fingers are released one by one; this is the oral instruction (*upadeśa*).

Then: *Oṃ vajrānala mahābhūta jvālaya sarvaṃ bhasmīkuru sarvaduṣṭān hūṃ phaṭ | dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ samayas tvaṃ samayo ’ham*—thus one should cause the pledge (*samaya*) to be heard three times. Then, from the deity: *Oṃ vajrānala mahābhūta jvālaya sarvaṃ bhasmīkuru sarvaduṣṭān hūṃ phaṭ | dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ samayo ’ham*—by this, recited three times, the pledge should be proclaimed. Then...
"The bowl is the transformation of the bell, and the *sruva* ladle is considered to be born from the vajra.
Having meditated thus, the knower of mantras should perform the oblation in this sequence.

"The bowl is the transformation of the bell, and the *sruva* ladle is considered to be born from the vajra. Having meditated thus, the knower of mantras should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) according to this sequence.
Having meditated upon a vessel filled with ghee with the left hand turned upward, one should likewise hold the spoon,
which is filled with ghee, turned upward, and resting upon the vessel.
With the left hand, hold the pouring ladle filled with clarified butter in the palm-up position; with the right hand, form a downward-facing fist to fill the dipping ladle with clarified butter.
Holding him with the supreme *bodhyagrī* [mudrā] by the left cheek with a fist,
and placing both hands between the knees, one should contemplate the supreme meditative absorption (*samādhi*) with a mind focused on concentration.
Having again placed the syllable *ruṃ* on the tongue at the mouth of the Vajra-fire,
one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) after causing [the vessel] to be circumambulated.

Furthermore, upon the mouth of the Vajra Fire God, one should place the syllable HŪṂ on the tongue; having performed the clockwise circumambulation with the offering ladle, one should present the burnt offerings in their entirety.

There, with this mantra: *Oṃ, to Agni, who blazes up again and again, enter, enter, for the sake of great glory, the bearer of the *havya* and *kavya* offerings, svāhā!*—one should offer three, seven, or twenty-one full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*) according to the capacity of the patron.

The mantra for this is as follows: *oṃ āgneye dīpya dīpya āviśa āviśa mahāśriye havyakavyabhānaya svāhā*. By means of this, the patron, through the power of his capacity, should offer three, seven, or twenty-one oblations of clarified butter.
Oṃ agnaye svāhā; this is the mantra for the other oblations of clarified butter.
*oṃ āgneye svāhā*. This is the mantra for the oblation of clarified butter (*ājya-homa*).

The four mudrās— the bowl, the sruva-ladle, the jewel, and the lotus— are prescribed for the grasping of vessels during rites such as pacification (śānti) and prosperity (puṣṭi), as well as for the four wrathful fists known as Bodhyaṅgī, Maṇi, Padma, and Krodha.

For the mantras of pacifying, enriching, and so forth, it is taught that one should hold the *darvī* and *śruk* ladles while assuming the four mudrās: the supreme enlightenment, the jewel, the lotus, and the wrathful fist.
In an act of malevolent sorcery (abhicāruka), one should offer oblations with pungent oil mixed with poison;
[this should be done] with a counter-clockwise rotation, in a state of wrath, and with the hands placed outside the knees.
One should perform the fire offering with hot sesame oil mixed with poison; for the wrathful deity, it is performed counter-clockwise, with the hand positioned behind the knee.
One should place upon the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) a vessel in the form of a thirty-two-petalled lotus;
having a slight opening and filled with ghee, it should drip from the tip of a blade of kuśa grass.
A vessel made of thirty-two lotus petals, filled with ghee and having a small opening, should be placed upon the hearth, dripping from the tip of a blade of kuśa grass.
One should perform the pouring of the stream of knowledge into the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍanābhi);
however, for a cruel or venomous [victim], the pouring should be done with pungent oil.
The stream of primordial wisdom should be made to descend into the center of the hearth; it flows intensely with hot sesame oil and poison.

At the mouths of the *pātrī* and *sruva* ladles, one should contemplate the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of one’s own deity interspersed with three syllables for the rites of pacification (*śānti*), nourishment (*puṣṭi*), subjugation (*vaśya*), and attraction (*ākarṣa*). One should recite at the end of the mantra: *svāhā*, *oṃ*, *hoḥ*, or *jaḥ*. However, for fierce (*krūra*) rites, one should recite *hūṃ hūṃ* or *phaṭ*. For fierce rites, the mouth [of the vessel] should be slightly opened; for the attraction of fierce beings, it should be opened very wide.

One should arrange the three syllables upon the ladle for filling and the ladle for pouring, and visualize them as arising from the seed-syllable of one’s own deity. For the rites of pacifying, enriching, magnetizing, and summoning through power, one should utter *svāhā*, *oṃ*, *hūḥ*, and *jaḥ* at the end of the mantra; however, for the wrathful rites, one should utter *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
With the mouth slightly opened, "fierce" and "forcibly summoning" refer to the mouth being very wide open.
Then, by means of the sign of the flame, one should discern the absence of obstacles and so forth:
it is radiant, turning to the right, glossy,
and likewise smokeless.
Resembling gold, silver, coral, and so forth, it has the shape of a fly-whisk;
it resembles a trident, a vajra, a conch,
a lotus, a fish, and a śrīvatsa.
Having the shapes of a water-pot, a svastika, an umbrella, a sword, a banner, and a *sruc* and *sruva* ladle;
deep with the sound of a drum, fragrant, and perfectly stainless.
"Resembling safflower and lapis lazuli, beautiful like Indra’s bow"—this was the general description; now the specific details are being told.

*Me tog bee d'urya 'dra dang || dbang po'i gzhu dang mtshungs rnams dge || zhes pa thun mong bstan pa ste || da ni khyad par brjod par bya ||* [The Tibetan text: "Resembling the flower *vaidūrya* and like Indra’s bow—these are auspicious. This was the general teaching; now the particulars shall be explained.
In pacification (*śāntika*), it appears white in color; in enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), it resembles yellow;
for subjugation (*vaśya*), it is red—the crest is most excellent; and for malevolent rites (*abhicāruka*), it is dark blue-black.
A single crest-lock is declared the best; two crest-locks are considered middling;
and three crest-locks should be known as inferior by the practitioner in brief.
The single-pointed [flame] is taught as supreme; the two-pointed is considered middling; the blazing-pointed is inferior. This should be understood in brief by the practitioner.
With its continuity interrupted, the flame is undesirable, possessing a harsh sound;

likewise, it emits sparks, has dim radiance, and is thick with smoke. It burns with difficulty, is unpleasant with its rough noise, scatters flying embers, and is similarly weak in light and abundant in smoke.
Having the odor of a corpse or a foul smell, with a rough color and a jagged crest, turning to the left, and having the shape of a fire licking the sacrificial ladle—

[these are the signs]. Having the odor of a corpse or a foul smell, with a rough color and a jagged crest, turning to the left, and having the shape of a fire licking the sacrificial ladle— [these are the signs].
But in a cruel act, an auspicious result may arise from inauspicious omens.

Having thus recognized the obstacle, one who performs all rites should personally sprinkle [it] with water; for it is auspicious for wrathful activities, as well as for non-virtuous ones. Having cleared away the obstructors through the Tathāgata, one should perform all the rites oneself.
Having performed the protection with that very [mantra], one should offer seven oblations of ghee.
Again, as before, with a vessel full of clarified butter and other substances while reciting the mantra,
one should offer three, seven, or even just one final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).

With those very same hands, one should offer seven oblations of clarified butter. Again, with mantras such as those for the butter, one should fill the offering-spoon as before; then, three, seven, or even just one complete oblation should be offered.

Therein, one should first purify the fuel sticks (*samidh*) and other materials with this: *oṃ āḥ hūṃ svāhā*. This is the purification of the fuel sticks. *oṃ śrīṃ svāhā*. This is the purification of the clarified butter (*ghṛta*). *oṃ svāhā*. This is the washing of the fragrant substances (*dravya*). *oṃ jrīṃ svāhā*. This is the purification of the rice (*vrīhi*). *oṃ kuru kuru svāhā*. This is the mantra for the purification of other materials.

First, one should purify the sacrificial wood and other materials with these mantras: *oṃ āḥ hūṃ svāhā*—this is for purifying the sacrificial wood (*samidh*). *oṃ śrīṃ svāhā*—this is for the clarified butter (*ghṛta*). *oṃ sva sva hā*—this is for washing the ritual substances. *oṃ jriṃ svāhā*—this is for purifying the grains. *oṃ kuru kuru svāhā*—this is the mantra for purifying other ritual substances.

The sequence here is as follows: having offered fuel-sticks into the kindled fire, one should offer clarified butter, sesame seeds, *dūrvā* grass, rice grains, curd-rice, and *kuśa* grass, and so forth.
Here, having burned the sacrificial wood in sequence, one should offer into the fire of the sacrificial wood sesame, parched grain, rice, curd-rice, *kuśa* grass, and so forth.

In this regard, the sequence for taking the fuel sticks (*samidh*) is as follows: one should take the fuel sticks and *dūrvā* grass or *kuśa* grass with the ring finger and thumb, while reciting the respective mantras that will be described hereafter.

Then, taking the *yaṃ* sticks in succession, one should take the *yaṃ* sticks, the *ūrṇā* grass, and the *kuśa* grass with the ring finger and the thumb using their respective mantras as will be explained.
Below and above, there shall be pacification (śānti) and likewise nourishment (pauṣṭika);
at the front, subjugation (vaśya) and attraction (ākarṣaṇa) shall be, as well as paralyzing (stambhana) and deluding (mohana).
Through the root and the tip, pacification and enrichment are likewise achieved; through the tip, mastery is attained, and likewise summoning; the same applies to paralyzing and stupefying.
Death is said to occur at the base portion, and eradication is considered to occur in the middle;
having understood this, one filled with compassion should perform the fire sacrifice according to the prescribed rule.

By means of the root part, death occurs; by the middle part, one intends to expel. Having understood this, one endowed with compassion should perform the fire offering (homa) according to the ritual procedure.

Oṃ vajrabrahmaṇe svāhā | [for] the *palāśa* tree. Oṃ vajrayajñāya svāhā | [for] the *udumbara* tree. Oṃ sahakārāya svāhā | [for] the *āmra* tree. Oṃ kadambāya svāhā | [for] the *kadamba* tree. Oṃ sarvatobhadrāya svāhā | [for] the *gambhārī* tree. Oṃ bodhivṛkṣāya svāhā | [for] the *aśvattha* tree. Oṃ vajralatāyai svāhā | [for] the *plakṣa* tree. Oṃ vajraśivāya svāhā | [for] the *śamī* tree. Oṃ vajrakuverāya svāhā | [for] the *nyagrodha* tree.

Oṃ vajragātrāya svāhā | [for wood] of the *khadira* tree. Oṃ vajrāśokāya svāhā | [for wood] of the *aśoka* tree. Oṃ vajralakucāya svāhā | [for wood] of the *lakuca* tree. Oṃ vajrārkāya svāhā | [for wood] of the *arka* tree. Oṃ vajraśruvāya svāhā | [for wood] of the *vaikaṅkata* tree. Oṃ vajrabhilloṭakāya svāhā | [for wood] of the *bhilloṭaka* tree. Oṃ vajramadanāya svāhā | [for wood] of the *madanakaṇṭaka* tree. Oṃ vajraśikharāya svāhā | [for wood] of the *apāmārga* tree. Oṃ vajrāṅkuśāya svāhā | [for wood] of all thorny trees.

oṃ vajrabrahmaṇe svāhā | This is the mantra of Pālaśī. oṃ vajrajñānāya svāhā | This is the mantra of Audumbarī. oṃ sahakārāya svāhā | This is the mantra of Āmrā. oṃ kadambāya svāhā | This is the mantra of Kadambī. oṃ sarvatobhadrāya svāhā | This is the mantra of Gambharī. oṃ bodhiprīkṣāya svāhā | This is the mantra of Aśvatthī. oṃ vajralatāya svāhā |

{213b2} For the *plakṣa* tree: Oṃ vajra śīva svāhā. For the *sami* tree: Oṃ vajra kūparya svāhā. For the *nyagrodha* tree: Oṃ gatrāya svāhā. For the *śrīparṇī* (khadira) tree: Oṃ vajra aśokāya svāhā. For the *aśoka* tree: Oṃ vajra lakuṭāya svāhā. For the *lakuṭa* tree: Oṃ vajra ārkāya svāhā. For the *arka* tree.

Oṃ vajrasruvāya svāhā! This is for the *be-kaṅki*. Oṃ vajrabilodhakāya svāhā! This is for the *bi-lo-dha-ka*. Oṃ vajramadanāya svāhā! This is for the intoxicating *tshe-rma-can* (thorny) tree. Oṃ vajraśikharāya svāhā! This is for the *āpa-marga*. Oṃ vajrāṅkuśāya svāhā! This is for all thorny trees.

Oṃ, to Agni, svāhā! To ghee, svāhā! Oṃ, to the Vajra that burns all sins, svāhā! To sesame seeds, svāhā! Oṃ, to Vajrāyus, svāhā! To dūrvā grass and kunda flowers, svāhā! Oṃ, to Vajrapuṣṭi, svāhā! To unbroken rice grains, svāhā! Oṃ, to all prosperity, svāhā! To curd-rice and milk-rice, svāhā! Oṃ, to the Unobstructed Vajra, svāhā! To kuśa grass smeared with sesame oil, svāhā! Oṃ, to Vajrabīja, svāhā! To grain, svāhā! Oṃ, to Vajravega, svāhā! To barley, svāhā!
Oṃ vajraghasmare svāhā | for wheat. Oṃ vajramahābalāya svāhā | for black gram. Oṃ vajralājāya svāhā | for parched grain.

Oṃ āgneye svāhā! This is for butter. Oṃ sarvapāpaṃ dahana vajrāya svāhā! This is for sesame seeds. Oṃ vajrāyushe svāhā! This is for durva grass and kuṇḍa flowers. Oṃ vajrapuṣṭaye svāhā! This is for unbroken grains of rice. Oṃ sarvasampade svāhā! This is for curd-rice, flour-rice, and the finest foods. Oṃ āpratihātāya svāhā!

For those *kuśa* grasses smeared with sesame oil: *oṃ vajravijaya svāhā*. For barley: *oṃ vajravigaya svāhā*. For wheat: *oṃ vajraghasmarīya svāhā*. For mung beans: *oṃ vajramahābalaya svāhā*. For parched rice: *oṃ vajralājaya svāhā*.
Alternatively, grains and so forth [should be offered] with the mantra of the deity to be propitiated.
Or else, for the purpose of satiation, [one should offer] salt and so forth with the deity's mantra.
As for the remaining substances, such as *priyaṅgu*, sandalwood,
and pills of *guggulu*, they should be offered with the mantra of the deity alone.

Those who know the traditional scriptures and possess great learning say that one should offer oblations with all substances intended for sacrifice, having sprinkled them with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) beginning with feces and thereby brought them to the state of nectar.

The masters who know the pith instructions and possess great erudition state that all substances to be burned should be sprinkled with the five nectars—such as those explained in the *Vyākhyā* and other texts—and one should perform the oblations while meditating on them as being the actual nature of nectar.
In all cases, liquid substances are [offered] into the mouth.
The fuel consists of human bone powder and so forth,
[to be placed] within the circle of light (*prabhāmaṇḍala*).
Curd-rice, food, water for rinsing the mouth, sesame, *dūrvā* grass,
and water are [offered] into the hand.
The fragrance is at the heart.
The scent is at the heart.
The flower is on the head.
{214a1} || The flower is upon the head.
Incense [is offered] into the flame. *Dhūpaṃ jvālāyām* | Incense is for the nose.
Water for the feet is for the two feet.
The lamp and the arghya offering [are placed] in front;
one should release the arghya water into the vessel (pātra).
The water for the offering to the preceptor should be poured into a vessel.

Thereafter, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and the sprinkling around (paryukṣaṇa), one should establish the fire in the south-eastern direction, either in the form of a flame within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or in its own essential form.

Following that, having performed the ritual washing of the feet and the sprinkling of the *bsang* offering, the Fire God (*Agnidevatā*), appearing in the form of a blazing flame, should be established in his own form within the hearth toward the southeast;
this is the procedure for the propitiation of the Fire God.
Thus concludes the ritual for pleasing the fire deity.
Having properly consecrated all the sacrificial implements with mantras and subsequently sprinkled them with water, he, being composed, places them within the midst of the fire.

The mantrin should perform all the necessary preparations for the fire offering exactly as taught, according to the ritual procedure, including the purification and sprinkling; then, once again remaining in meditative equipoise, [he should act] in the midst of the fire.
Having meditated according to the nature of the rite upon the eternal [deities] and others in accordance with the rule,
and having performed the invocation and other rites, one should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and so forth as before.

Having contemplated the ritual procedures for the permanent [deities] and so forth in accordance with the rite, and having formed the intention that accords with the activity, one should offer the external substances and so forth, such as the items to be burned, as previously described.
And at the very end, having recited twenty-one, seventy,
and three oblations of clarified butter, one should cause the heart of the presiding lord to blaze up with the [presiding] heart-mantra.
Finally, at the end of all [the mantras], one should kindle the fire with clarified butter oblations recited twenty-one, seven, or likewise three times, using the essence-mantra of the Lord.
Afterwards, the practitioner, being well-composed, should offer the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) recited over by the presiding deity,
and likewise offer the guest-water (argha), having consecrated it with that same mantra.

Furthermore, by reciting the heart mantra of the Lord, one should perform the fire offering with full oblations; remaining in perfect meditative equipoise, one should recite that very essence and, as one committed to the ascetic observances, present the water for the feet.

Then, having sprinkled water around [the deity], offered water for sipping (ācamana), a new cloth, and betel-leaf without lime (cūrṇa)—though in a rite of a cruel nature, it is with lime—having worshipped, praised, and prostrated as before, and having offered the arghya, one should ask the Blessed One for forgiveness while reciting: "With my hands joined in a hollowed cup holding flowers placed at my heart, may I ask the Blessed One for forgiveness to pacify defects such as omissions."

Then, having offered the *bsang gtor* (fumigation offering), the water for rinsing the mouth, new garments, and tooth-wood—without powdered stone for fierce rites—or with powdered stone for fierce rites, one should worship, praise, and prostrate as before. Having presented the honorarium (*dakṣiṇā*), one should join the palms at the heart together with flowers and speak these words in order to request the Blessed One’s forgiveness:
Whatever evil has been done by me again through my deluded mind,
that must be forgiven by you, O Lord, for you are the protector of all embodied beings.
Whatever slight misdeeds I have committed through my deluded mind, may you, O Protector, forgive them all, for you are the refuge of all embodied beings.
O Leader, whatever duty was not performed here due to lack of attainment, lack of full understanding, or lack of capability, you ought to forgive all of that.
Whatever has been done here out of failure to find [the right person], lack of full understanding, or simply being unable [to do it], it is fitting that the Lord should forgive all of that.

Having thus asked for forgiveness, and having entreated [the deities] for the accomplishment of one's desired aims, one should recite "Oṃ Vajrasattva Āḥ" many times with the aspiration for liberation in order to pacify the faults of deficiency or excess, and then recite the hundred-syllable mantra.

Oṃ Vajrasattva, maintain your pledge; abide as Vajrasattva; be firm for me, be well-pleased with me, be well-nourished by me, be devoted to me; grant me all accomplishments, and in all actions, make my mind auspicious! Hūṃ ha ha ha ha ho! O Blessed One, Vajra of all Tathāgatas, do not abandon me; become the Vajra; O Great Samaya-being! Āḥ!

Having thus requested forbearance, one should offer a supplication for the sake of accomplishing one's desired aims and recite "Oṃ vajrasattva āḥ" many times with the intention of liberation, in order to pacify the faults of omissions and excesses; then one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra: Oṃ vajrasattva samayam anupālaya | vajrasattva tvenopatiṣṭha dṛḍho me bhava |

*Su-to-śyo-me-bhava | Su-po-śyo-me-bhava | Ānu-rakto-me-bhava | Sarva-siddhiṃ me prayaccha | Sarva-karmasu ca me cittaṃ śreyah kuru hūṃ ha ha ha ha ho bhagavān sarvatathāgata-vajra-māme muñca vajrī bhava mahāsamayasattva āḥ.* Then,
following that:
The welfare of all sentient beings has been accomplished by you, and the appropriate siddhi has been granted. Go to the realm of the Buddhas, and may you return once again!
You have performed every benefit for sentient beings; grant the corresponding accomplishments (*anugā-siddhi*). Having gone to the domain of the Buddhas, please return once more.
Having thus exhorted [him], while reciting one's own mantra ending with the three syllables and concluding with the syllable *muḥ*, one should mentally dismiss the Lord, one's own sovereign.

Having thus exhorted [the deity] correctly, one should recite the syllable *muḥ* at the end of the three syllables of one’s own mantra placed within [the heart], and mentally request one’s own lord, the Protector, to depart according to the ritual procedure.

Then, having placed the fire in the hearth, worshipped it again, and sprinkled water around it, one should offer water for rinsing the mouth and betel-leaf without lime; however, in the case of a cruel rite, it should be with lime. Having given a new cloth and offered the remaining sacrificial implements, one should at the conclusion praise [the deity] while ringing a bell, reciting the verses beginning with "Akṣobhyavajra... and so forth.

Then, having invited the fire deity into the hearth and once again made perfect offerings, one should present the *gandha* (fumigation), the *ācamana* (water for rinsing the mouth), and tooth-cleansing paste—without powdered stone for peaceful rites, but with powdered stone for wrathful ones—as well as new garments.
Having performed the *homa* with the remaining ritual implements, one should ring the bell and offer praise with the verses beginning with "Akṣobhyavajra."
This procedure is generally for one who has set out to accomplish a desired siddhi.

However, regarding the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and other rites for one who delights in the welfare of others, this is the distinction: having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the disciple, the preceptor takes the disciple’s left big toe with his own left little finger, circumambulates the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) three times clockwise, and while lowering [the toe] clockwise from the head with the *sruva* ladle, he offers seven oblations and then causes the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) to be offered.

The distinction for those who desire the welfare of others, such as the consecration and so forth, is as follows: having grasped the little finger of the left hand of the disciple who has offered the ritual fee, one should circumambulate the fire-pit three times to the right and, using the pouring ladle, apply [the substance] to the head while circling to the right; thus, one should perform the burnt offering seven times and cause the disciple to present a full offering.
Having tied the *pratisara* mantra, recited over the *kuṇḍalinī*, to his hand, he should sprinkle water around [the sacrificial ground].
Having wound that protective cord, which has been consecrated by recitation, around the person's arm, one should perform the purification sprinkling (bsang gtor).

When such an occasion arises, one should offer a full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for the sake of the prosperity of the king and others. As it has been said: "One should duly offer three oblations or one for each of the king, the world-protectors (lokapālas), all sentient beings, the disciples, and certain other favored individuals; and one should cause a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given."

If [the deity] is present, one should offer the completed oblations while focusing on the virtues of the king and others. Thus it is said: "One should perform the oblation three times for each—the king, the world-protectors, all sentient beings, and whoever is desired—and likewise cause the ritual fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to be offered according to the ritual procedure."

Thereafter, having offered water for sipping (ācamana), sprinkled water around [the deity], worshipped [him], and offered the guest-offering (argha), having asked for forgiveness and entreated [the deity] for the attainment of one's desired goal, one should recite "oṃ vajrasattva āḥ," urge [the deity] to depart as before, and dismiss [him] according to the ritual rules while reciting "oṃ mur."

Following that, having offered water for rinsing the mouth, one should perform the *bsang gtor* (fumigation offering), present perfect worship, and offer the *argha* (water for honor). Having requested forbearance and petitioned for the desired accomplishments (*siddhi*), one should urge [the deity] to depart as before by reciting "Oṃ vajrasattva āḥ," and then request them to depart according to the ritual procedure while reciting "Oṃ muḥ."
In this manner, one should perform [the practice] once daily, or at the three junctions of the day, or at the four junctions.
Thus, one should practice every day, or at the time of explanation, or in three sessions, or in four sessions.

Then, having poured milk, sugar-candy, rice, ghee, honey, and sugar into a vessel with a *sruva* ladle—or in its absence, using a *pippala* leaf—and having placed it upon a copper or other metal cooking-pot situated on a tripod (*yantrikā*) while holding his fingers together, he should take a garland along with a bell in his left hand and the *akṣasūtra* transformed into a vajra in his right hand; then, reciting the mantra with the visualization (*bhāvanā*) of making it nectar, he should prepare the milk-rice (*pāyasa*) in the form of nectar within the fire of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), [the pot] being smeared with fragrances appropriate for the rite and having a garland tied around its neck.
The yogin, being composed in meditative absorption, should partake [of the offering] for each respective deity, the world-protectors, and himself.

Then, with the fingers properly extended and joined, one should pour milk, unhusked rice, clarified butter, honey, and molasses using a large and small ladle; or, if these are unavailable, one should pour *tsharu* (a type of medicinal paste) into a copper vessel or similar object placed upon the hearth, using *āpplā* leaves or fingers properly extended and joined. And [the ritual] action...

Having applied the appropriate unguents and tied a flower garland around the neck, one should hold the garland together with a bell in the left hand; then, visualizing that the rosary and vajra in the right hand have been transformed into nectar, one should recite the mantra.

Having completed the preparation of the milk porridge in the nature of nectar, one should satisfy the deities, the world-protectors, oneself, and the patrons by entering meditative equipoise in yoga, just as [one satisfies] the fire in the hearth.
"Eat this, the remnant of the Tathāgata; it destroys all evil. (idaṃ tāthāgataṃ śeṣaṃ bhuṅkṣva pāpavināśanam)
Thus the teacher should say; he should then distribute the remainder among those who request it.
Thus the master should speak, and he should also distribute the remainder to those who desire it.
The extinguishing of the fire with milk is for pacification; with milk for the accomplishment of nourishment;
with yellow water for subjugation; and with white or black milk for the cruel rites.
For pacifying, one should use milk; for enriching, yellow water; for magnetizing, red milk; and for the wrathful, black [milk].
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the fire offering (homa) that satiates the external deities.
Thus concludes the ritual for the external fire offering (*bāhyahomavidhi*) for the purpose of pleasing the deity.

One should perform all this with the mind through meditative cultivation exactly as it is, neither deficient nor redundant; thus, the desired goal will certainly be accomplished. This is the mental fire-offering (*homa*) independent of external objects. Possessing the yoga of one's chosen deity, one should—according to the sequence of the purification of one's own nature—fearlessly enjoy the five objects of desire, such as form and so forth, which are of the nature of Vairocana and the other [Buddhas], or of the nature of Vajrasattva, as they arise.

At the time of eating, however, one should purify one’s own food through the equality of all things and transform it into nectar (*amṛta*). Then, having embraced the fire of the navel-pit, one should duly satisfy the circle of one’s chosen deities (*iṣṭadevatā*) residing in the heart by means of the hands as a vessel and so forth. As it is said: "If one meditates mentally such that all these [offerings] are without deficiency or excess, one's desired goals will certainly be fulfilled. Thus, the mental fire-offering (*manohoma*) is performed without depending on external objects.

Possessing the yoga of one’s own chosen deity, one should—either through its essence, or in the form of Vajrasattva, or according to the sequence of one's own respective purified natures as the essence of Vairocana and so forth—infallibly enjoy the five objects of desire, such as forms and so on, exactly as they are obtained.

At the time of eating, one should transform all of one’s food into the purity of nectar through equanimity, and then, using the fire in the hearth of the navel as a means of embrace, one should properly satisfy the wheel of the gods of the impure desire residing in the heart with the ladle of the hands and so forth, according to the ritual procedure.
This is the method for the internal fire-offering (*adhyātma-homa*) by means of external substances. || [Symbol] ||
Thus concludes the ritual for the inner fire offering using external substances.
